Skill version: 0.1 Student: calvin Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-14

AI: Here is a question to start us off — no LCA knowledge needed yet.
Imagine you are reviewing a restaurant receipt at the end of a work dinner. The receipt shows the food and drinks your table ordered — but it does not include the taxi you took to get there, the parking fee your colleague paid, or the round of drinks someone bought at the bar next door.
If someone added up only the restaurant receipt to figure out the total cost of the evening, would that number be accurate — and what would be missing from it?
Student: it would be missing the taxi and parking costs
AI: Exactly right — the receipt only covers what happened inside that restaurant. The taxi, the parking, the drinks next door — all of those were real costs that actually happened that evening, but because they were outside the restaurant’s bill, they simply do not appear. The total on the receipt is not wrong, but it is incomplete.
Life Cycle Assessment works the same way. Every study has its own version of that receipt — a defined set of steps it covers and a defined set it does not. That defined edge is called the system boundary (meaning: the line that separates what is counted from what is not). Everything inside the boundary is measured and added up. Everything outside is ignored, even if it causes real environmental harm.
Now let’s look at a real example. This study is called the Polyester T-shirt. Its goal is to calculate the climate impact of producing one T-shirt, tracing the journey from crude oil in the ground all the way to a finished garment ready for sale.
Here is the supply chain diagram — each box is a step that this study decided to include:
 ../../skills_references/polyester_tshirt/product_graph_structure.svg
The fence — the system boundary — runs around all three of those boxes together. Any step not shown in the diagram is outside the fence and was not counted.
Looking at the diagram, can you think of anything that happens to the T-shirt after it leaves the last box that might also cause environmental impact — but is not shown here?
Student: washing and drying it
AI: Exactly right — and that is a really important observation.
Every time a customer washes and tumble-dries a polyester T-shirt, that machine is using electricity and heating water, which releases CO₂. Over the lifetime of a T-shirt — which might be washed 50 or 100 times — that adds up to a significant amount of environmental impact. But none of that is captured in this study, because the boundary stops the moment the shirt leaves the factory.
This study is what’s called cradle to gate — meaning it starts at the very beginning of the supply chain (the oil well, which is the “cradle”) and stops at the factory exit (the “gate”). Everything that happens after the gate — the shop, the customer’s wardrobe, the washing machine, the bin — is outside the fence.
Here is the what-if question: if this study had included all those washes and tumble-dry cycles over the T-shirt’s lifetime, do you think the total carbon footprint would go up a little, or a lot — and why?

title: /life-cycle-stages wool_yarn
text:
/life-cycle-stages wool_yarn
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-14

AI: Here is a quick question before we look at any LCA numbers.
Imagine two friends both track their spending for a month. One tracks everything — rent, food, transport, nights out, the lot. The other only tracks their grocery bills. At the end of the month, who spent less?
The one who only tracked groceries — obviously. But is that a fair comparison?
Student: no it’s not fair
AI: Exactly — they were measuring different things. One covered the full picture, the other covered only a slice of it. The grocery number is not wrong, but you cannot compare it to the full-spending number and draw any conclusion about who is better at managing money.
In LCA, the same problem comes up constantly. Researchers have agreed on four standard ways to draw the fence — four named boundary types that describe where a study starts and where it stops. These are called life cycle stages (meaning: the named phases of a product’s life that a study can choose to include or exclude).
Knowing which stage a study covers is the first thing to check before you trust any footprint number — because the same product will get a completely different result depending on which stages are inside the fence.
Let’s go through all four using wool yarn as our example. Here is the first one:
Cradle to gate — this boundary starts at the very beginning of the supply chain, where the raw material comes from (the “cradle”) and stops at the factory exit (the “gate”). For wool yarn, that means the study covers the sheep farm and the yarn production mill — and nothing else. What happens to the yarn after it leaves the mill is outside the fence.
Before I go on — why do you think most supplier sustainability reports use cradle to gate rather than a wider boundary?
Student: because they can only control what happens on their side
AI: Exactly right — and that is a really important insight.
A wool yarn supplier controls the sheep farm and the mill. They have no control over what a fashion brand does with the yarn after they buy it — whether they knit it into a jumper, how that jumper gets washed, or where it ends up at the end of its life. It would not be fair to hold them responsible for impacts they cannot influence.
Now the other three boundary types, quickly:
Cradle to grave — starts at the same place as cradle to gate (the sheep farm) but continues all the way through to the very end of the product’s life. For a wool jumper made from this yarn, that would add the garment factory, the customer wearing and washing it for years, and eventually donating or disposing of it. This gives the most complete picture but requires estimates about consumer behaviour that can be hard to get right.
Cradle to cradle — the same as cradle to grave, but instead of ending at a bin, the end-of-life material loops back into production as recycled input. For wool, this could mean old garments being collected, shredded, and re-spun into new yarn — completing the circle.
Gate to grave — the opposite of cradle to gate. It starts at the warehouse or retail store and covers only what happens after purchase: the customer using the product and eventually disposing of it. All the production upstream is left out.
Here is the wool yarn supply chain diagram:
 ../../skills_references/wool_yarn/product_graph_structure.svg
The two boxes shown — sheep farming and yarn production — are everything this study included. Based on the four boundary types we just covered, which one does this diagram represent?
Student: cradle to gate
AI: Correct — and you can see exactly why just by looking at the diagram. The study starts at the sheep farm (the cradle) and ends when the finished yarn leaves the mill (the gate). Nothing after that point appears in the diagram, which means nothing after that point was counted.
Here is the what-if question: if a garment brand bought this wool yarn and wanted to do a cradle-to-grave study of the finished jumper — including the customer wearing it, hand-washing it, and eventually donating it to a charity shop — what extra steps would they need to add inside the fence that are not shown in that diagram?
Student: the garment factory, washing at home, and disposing of it
AI: Perfect — that is exactly the three things that would need to be added, and in the right order too.
This is the key insight the whole skill has been building toward: the same wool yarn has a different footprint number depending on which boundary you use. The cradle-to-gate number only reflects the farm and the mill. The cradle-to-grave number adds the garment factory, decades of home washing, and end-of-life disposal — and for a wool jumper that gets washed regularly over many years, that additional impact is not small.
This is why, when a supplier hands you a footprint number, the first question to ask is not “is that number high or low?” — it is “which boundary does that number cover?” A cradle-to-gate number and a cradle-to-grave number for the same product are not comparable, even if they are sitting side by side on the same page.
Would you like to move on to goal and scope — the full set of opening decisions every LCA study makes, of which boundary type is just one part? Or is there anything about the four boundary types you would like to look at more closely?

title: /goal-and-scope cotton_fiber
text:
/goal-and-scope cotton_fiber
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-13

AI: A cotton supplier wants to share a sustainability report with their fashion brand buyers. They need to decide what to include in the carbon footprint study. Should the study start from the fertilizer factory that makes the chemicals used on the farm — or is it enough to start from the cotton field itself, and treat the fertilizer as something that just “arrives”?
Where would you draw the line, and why?
Student: from the fertilizer factory
AI: That is a really practical instinct — and it is exactly the choice this study makes. Here is why it matters: the fertilizer factory turns out to be responsible for a significant chunk of the carbon footprint, so leaving it out would give buyers a falsely clean picture of how cotton is actually produced. You picked the more honest starting point.
The study we will work through is called Cotton Fiber — 1 kg. It calculates the environmental impact of producing 1 kg of ginned cotton fiber — that is, cotton that has had the seeds removed and is ready to be spun into yarn. It is a teaching example built for this course, with numbers calibrated to be realistic for irrigated cotton farming systems.
Here is the shape of the supply chain the study includes:
 ../../skills_references/cotton_fiber/product_graph_structure.svg
Two boxes, two steps. Each box represents a step the researchers decided to include in the study — and choosing which boxes belong inside the picture is exactly what scope means in LCA. The fertilizer factory is in there because you — and the researchers — agreed it should be.
Ready to hear about the two big questions every LCA has to answer before a single number gets calculated?
Student: yes
AI: Every LCA study has to answer two questions right at the start. Together they are called the goal and scope — and they are written down before any numbers are calculated, so that anyone reading the results later knows exactly what they are looking at.
The goal is the “why” and the “who.” In LCA, the goal is a short statement that says why the study is being done and who it is for — it matters because the same product can have a very different study design depending on whether the results are for an internal decision, a public label, or a legal certification. For this cotton study, the goal is: to calculate the climate and eutrophication impact of producing 1 kg of cotton fiber, so that buyers can understand what the supply chain actually contributes to environmental damage. The audience is a fashion brand sourcing team — people like you — comparing supplier claims.
The scope is the “what is in and what is out.” Think of it like a fence drawn around the supply chain — everything inside the fence is studied, everything outside is ignored. For this study, the fence encloses two steps: P1 — Fertilizer production and P2 — Cotton farming. The study stops the moment the cotton fiber leaves the farm gate, ready for spinning. What happens after that — transport, spinning, weaving, garment manufacturing — is outside the fence. This type of scope has a name: cradle to gate, meaning from the raw material in the ground all the way to the factory exit, but no further.
Does that distinction between goal and scope make sense so far — or would it help to have an example of what a different goal might look like for the same product?
Student: go ahead
AI: Here is something worth thinking about — a small change to the scope that would have a big effect on the result.
This study leaves out pesticides and herbicides — the chemicals sprayed on cotton fields to kill insects and weeds. Producing those chemicals takes energy and releases CO₂, just like the fertilizer factory does. The researchers made a deliberate choice to exclude them in order to keep the study simple and focused on nitrogen chemistry.
What if a competing cotton supplier ran their LCA and also left out pesticides — but their farming system actually uses more pesticide than yours? Their footprint number would look similar to yours on paper, even though their real-world impact is higher.
Do you think that kind of gap — where two studies use the same scope label (“cradle to gate”) but quietly exclude different things — could make supplier comparisons misleading?
Student: yes
AI: Exactly right — and this is one of the most important things to understand about sustainability data in fashion sourcing.
Two suppliers can both hand you a “cradle to gate” LCA and show similar numbers, while one has quietly excluded pesticides, transport, or seed production, and the other has included them. The label sounds the same but the fence is drawn in a different place. Without checking what is actually inside the fence, you cannot compare the two numbers fairly at all.
This is why, as a buyer or merchandiser, the first question to ask when a supplier shares an LCA result is not “what is the number?” — it is “what is inside the system boundary?” Sustainability certifications like the Higg Index or the European Environmental Footprint exist partly to solve this problem by forcing all suppliers to draw the fence in the same place, so comparisons are actually fair.
A number without a clearly stated scope is not evidence — it is just a number.

That wraps up the five steps for cotton fiber! Would you like to see how goal and scope decisions play out in a different context — for example, a footwear study or a retail logistics scenario?
Student: can you give me some examples other than this one?
AI: Absolutely! Here are two examples from very different parts of the retail world.

Example 1 — Footwear
A trainer brand runs an LCA on a running shoe. Their goal is to reduce the product’s footprint for an upcoming sustainability campaign aimed at consumers. Because the audience is the public — not a sourcing team — they need to include the full life of the shoe, not just manufacturing.
So their scope is cradle to grave: raw materials, factory, transport to store, the customer wearing and washing the shoes over two years, and finally disposal or recycling. If they had stopped at the factory gate (cradle to gate), the study would have missed the fact that the rubber sole releases microplastics during use — which turns out to be a significant part of the story.

Example 2 — E-commerce packaging
An online retailer wants to cut packaging waste. Their goal is to compare a cardboard box to a reusable fabric mailer — not to reduce production emissions, but to reduce what ends up in landfill. Because the question is about what happens after the customer receives the parcel, the scope they choose is gate to grave: it starts at the warehouse and ends when the packaging is thrown away or returned. The factory that made the cardboard is outside the fence — irrelevant to the decision they are trying to make.

Both examples show the same principle: the goal drives the scope. Change the question you are trying to answer, and the fence moves.
Would you like to explore another example, or does this feel like a good place to wrap up?

AI: Before we look at any numbers — imagine you’re a sourcing manager at a fashion brand, and two cotton suppliers both send you a data sheet claiming their cotton has a lower carbon footprint. What is the very first question you would ask before you could even start comparing those two numbers?
Student: what unit was used
AI: Exactly right — that is the single most important question, and experienced sustainability professionals ask it every time.
If one supplier measured their footprint per kilogram of cotton and the other measured it per bale (a bale is roughly 220 kg), the numbers are completely incomparable — even if the underlying environmental impact is identical. You’d be looking at 5.6 vs 1,232 and thinking one is catastrophically worse, when really they’re the same.
That instinct — per what? — is the entire concept we’re about to explore.
The study we’ll be working through is called Cotton Fiber — 1 kg. The goal is to calculate the climate impact of producing cotton fiber, tracing the supply chain all the way back from the cotton field to the fertilizer factory that supplies it. It’s a teaching example built for this course, so the numbers are illustrative rather than from a specific brand — but they’re calibrated to be realistic for irrigated cotton systems.
Here’s the shape of the supply chain:
 ../../skills_references/cotton_fiber/product_graph_structure.svg
You can see two boxes connected by an arrow. The rightmost box — P2 — Cotton farming — has a special name in LCA: it’s called the reference process. That just means it’s the finishing line — the step that delivers the finished product. Everything to its left exists only to supply it. The fertilizer factory (P1) is there for one reason only: to feed the cotton farm.
The functional unit is precisely what comes out of that reference process box.
What do you think comes out of P2? What is the cotton farm actually delivering?
Student: the fiber
AI: Exactly — the fiber. That’s the finished product this entire supply chain exists to produce.
So here is the functional unit for this study, stated precisely:

1 kg of ginned cotton fiber, ready for spinning

In LCA, this is called the functional unit — it is the precise definition of exactly what is being measured, so that comparisons between products are fair.
Notice how specific it is. Not just “cotton” — but ginned cotton (meaning the seeds have already been removed), and ready for spinning (meaning it’s in the form a textile mill would actually receive and use). That level of precision matters: if one supplier measures at the farm gate before ginning, and another measures after, you’re still not comparing the same thing.
Why 1 kg specifically? Because at the raw material stage, buyers and suppliers deal in weight. A sourcing manager comparing two fiber suppliers will ask: for every kilogram I buy, what is the environmental cost? It’s a natural, neutral unit for material-level comparisons — before the fiber becomes yarn, fabric, or a finished garment.
What it rules out: measuring per bale, per field, or per growing season — all of which would make comparisons between farms of different sizes completely meaningless.
Suppose a competing cotton supplier claims their fiber has a footprint of only 2.1 kg CO₂ — lower than the 5.6 kg CO₂ in this study. But when you read the fine print, you discover they measured per kg of raw seed cotton, before ginning — and it takes roughly 3 kg of seed cotton to produce 1 kg of ginned fiber. Would their number still look better once you account for that?

That one phrase does a lot of work. It tells you the quantity (1 kg), the product (wool yarn), and the condition it must be in (ready to use). A supplier who delivers tangled raw fleece doesn’t count — it has to be finished yarn.

Meanwhile, your yarn might go into heavy winter knitwear using 600g per sweater, so your “per sweater” number looks three times worse — through no fault of your production process at all.
This is why unit choice is never neutral. A supplier, a brand, or even a certification body can make a product look more or less sustainable just by choosing a different measuring stick — without changing a single thing about how it is made.
So as a buyer or merchandiser, the very first question to ask when a supplier hands you a sustainability certificate is: “Per what unit?” A carbon number without a clear unit attached to it is not a claim you can act on — it is just a number.

title: /system-boundary cotton_fiber
text:
/system-boundary cotton_fiber
Skill version: 0.1 Student: calvin Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-14

AI: Imagine you are reviewing a restaurant receipt at the end of a work dinner. The receipt only shows the food and drinks your table ordered — it does not include the taxi you took to get there, the parking fee your colleague paid, or the round of drinks someone bought at the bar next door.
Here’s the question: if someone added up only the restaurant receipt to figure out the total cost of the evening, would that number be accurate — and what would be missing from it?
Student: no it would not
AI: You’ve got it — and that gap between the receipt and the full picture is the central tension in LCA too.
In Life Cycle Assessment, every study has a “receipt” — a defined set of steps it covers and a defined set it does not. That boundary is called the system boundary. Think of it as a fence drawn around part of the supply chain. Everything inside the fence is measured and counted. Everything outside the fence is ignored — even if it causes real environmental harm.
The system boundary is not a flaw — it is a deliberate choice. But it means the number you get at the end of a study only tells you about what was inside the fence.
Let’s look at a real example — a study of Cotton Fiber. The goal is to calculate the environmental impact of producing 1 kg of ginned cotton fiber, tracing the supply chain from the fertilizer factory through to the cotton farm.
Here is the supply chain diagram:
 ../../skills_references/cotton_fiber/product_graph_structure.svg
Each box in this diagram is a step the study decided to include. The fence — the system boundary — runs around both of these boxes together. Any step that does not appear is outside the fence and was not counted.
Looking at the diagram, can you spot any steps you might expect to be there that are not shown? For example — think about what the cotton farm needs to operate beyond fertilizer. What else goes into growing cotton that might have its own environmental footprint?
Student: harvesting, pesticides
AI: Exactly right — and those are two really important ones.
Pesticides and herbicides have to be manufactured in a chemical factory before they ever arrive at the farm — and that manufacturing process uses energy and releases emissions. But in this study, the production of pesticides is completely outside the fence. The study includes the fertilizer factory but stops there — the pesticide factory is not shown in the diagram and was not counted at all.
Harvesting is similar — the diesel fuel burned by the harvesting machinery does appear indirectly (it is folded into the CO₂ figure for the cotton farm), but the manufacturing of the harvesting machine itself was left out.
Here is the what-if question: if the study had also included the production of all the pesticides and herbicides used on the farm — which had to be manufactured somewhere before they arrived — do you think the total carbon footprint would look bigger or smaller than the number this study reports?
Student: bigger
AI: Exactly — every time you pull something from outside the fence and bring it inside, the number goes up.
And this matters in a very practical way for anyone working in fashion or retail. Cotton has a reputation as a “natural” fiber — grown in a field, not made in a chemical plant. But this study already shows that just the fertilizer factory alone adds significantly to the footprint. If you also counted the pesticide factories, the seed production, the transport to the spinning mill, and eventually the disposal of the finished garment, the number would keep climbing with every step you added.
When a cotton supplier hands you an LCA result, the system boundary is the first thing to check — not the number. Two suppliers can report very different footprints for the same cotton simply because one drew a wider fence than the other. You can only compare them fairly if they used the same boundary — otherwise you are comparing two different receipts and assuming they cover the same meal.
The system boundary is one decision inside a bigger set called goal and scope — the opening chapter of every LCA study, where researchers decide why the study is being done, who it is for, and exactly where the fence gets drawn. Would you like to explore how boundary decisions fit into that bigger goal-and-scope picture, or is there anything about the boundary concept you’d like to dig into first?
Student: can people fudge the system boundary
AI: This is a really good question — and the honest answer is yes, it happens.
It is not always outright lying. The most common version is simply choosing a conveniently narrow boundary and either not mentioning it clearly, or burying it in the fine print. A cotton supplier might publish a footprint number that only covers the farm itself — leaving out the fertilizer factory entirely — because that makes the number look smaller. Nothing in the report is technically false, but the reader walks away with an incomplete picture.
This is one of the main mechanisms behind greenwashing — making a product look more sustainable than it really is, not by inventing data, but by carefully choosing where the fence goes. In our cotton example, the fertilizer factory alone contributes about 0.7 kg of CO₂ equivalent per kg of cotton. Leave that out, and the footprint suddenly looks much more flattering.
The defence against this — both as a buyer and as a brand manager — is always to ask the same two questions when you see an LCA number: “What is inside the fence?” and “What did you leave out, and why?” A trustworthy study will answer both questions clearly and upfront.

Let’s look at a real example — a study of Wool Yarn. The goal is to calculate the climate impact of producing 1 kg of wool yarn, tracing the supply chain from sheep farming through to the spinning mill.
Here is the supply chain diagram for this study:

Each box in this diagram is a step the study decided to include. The fence — the system boundary — runs around both of these boxes. Any step that does not appear is outside the fence and was not counted.

Every single one of those steps uses energy and causes some environmental impact — but none of them appear in this diagram, because they are all outside the fence.
This study’s boundary stops the moment the finished yarn leaves the mill. That is a common choice called cradle to gate — it covers everything from the sheep farm (the “cradle”) up to the exit of the last factory (the “gate”), and nothing after.
Here is the what-if question: what if the boundary had also included the energy used to transport the yarn to a garment factory, and then the garment factory itself — the cutting, sewing, and finishing of a finished sweater? Do you think the total carbon footprint number would go up, go down, or stay the same — and why?

Every time you widen the fence to include more steps, the number goes up — because you are counting more real activity that causes real emissions. A narrow boundary will always produce a smaller number than a wide one, even if they are studying the same product.
This matters enormously in a business context. When a wool supplier hands you an LCA result showing a low carbon footprint, the system boundary is the first thing to check — not the number. Two suppliers can report very different footprints for the same material simply because one drew a wider fence than the other. Neither number is necessarily wrong, but they are not the same thing, and you cannot compare them directly.
The system boundary is one decision inside a bigger set called goal and scope — the opening chapter of every LCA study, where researchers decide why the study is being done, who it is for, and exactly where the fence gets drawn. A wool producer might publish a cradle-to-gate number that stops at the mill gate, while an environmental group might argue that the study should have gone all the way to end-of-life disposal. Both are using real data — but because the fences are drawn in different places, they get very different numbers, and each side can accuse the other of cherry-picking.
This is also where greenwashing can happen — not necessarily through lying, but through choosing a conveniently narrow boundary and not being upfront about it. A brand might advertise “our wool sweater has a footprint of only 2 kg CO₂” — but if that number only covers the final spinning mill and nothing else, it leaves out the sheep farm, which in our wool yarn example is responsible for roughly 86% of the total impact.
So the practical skill for someone in fashion buying or brand management is not to memorise carbon numbers — it is to always ask: “What is inside the fence, and what did you leave out?”

title: /technosphere-and-ecosphere wool_yarn
text:
/technosphere-and-ecosphere wool_yarn
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-15

AI: Imagine a busy town that has a wall around it. Inside the wall: houses, factories, shops, roads — everything built and run by people. Outside the wall: fields, rivers, the sky, the forest — nature, exactly as it would be without humans.
Now imagine a factory inside the wall burns coal to run its machines. Two things happen: first, a truck drives through the town and delivers the coal (that coal never leaves the wall — it moves from one part of the human world to another). Second, the chimney sends smoke up into the sky above the wall — and that smoke drifts out beyond the wall into the fields and the river.
Here is the question: which of those two things — the coal truck or the chimney smoke — actually crosses the wall and reaches the natural world outside?
Student: chimney smoke
AI: Exactly — the coal truck stayed inside the town the whole time. It moved from a coal yard to a factory, but it never left the human-made world. The chimney smoke is the one that crossed the wall and drifted out into the fields and the river. That crossing is where environmental harm begins.
In Life Cycle Assessment, researchers use two names for these two worlds. The human-made world — everything inside the wall, like factories, farms, mills, and trucks — is called the technosphere (from “techno”, meaning made by people). The natural world outside the wall — air, water, soil, living ecosystems — is called the ecosphere (from “eco”, meaning the living environment).
The most important idea in LCA is this: environmental harm only happens when something crosses the boundary between the two. Emissions released into the ecosphere (like CO₂ into the air) and resources pulled out of the ecosphere (like water from a river) are the flows that cause impact. Everything that moves around inside the technosphere — a bag of raw wool travelling from a farm to a mill, say — stays inside the wall and does not directly harm the natural world.
Now let’s sort a real LCA study into these two worlds. This is the recipe card for Wool Yarn — 1 kg.
 ../../skills_references/wool_yarn/product_graph_structure.svg
Inside the wall — the technosphere: The two boxes in this diagram are the processes — the human activities that make the yarn. In this study that means Sheep farming and Wool yarn production. Also inside the wall is the intermediate product flowing between those two boxes: Raw wool passing from the farm to the mill. That flow stays entirely inside the human-made world. It does not touch nature.
Crossing the wall — into and out of the ecosphere: Two types of flows cross the boundary in this study: - Emissions going out into nature: Carbon dioxide and Methane, both released to air. These are substances the processes produce and discharge into the natural world. - Resources coming in from nature: Water, drawn from a natural water source to run the scouring and spinning operations.
In LCA, these crossings are called elementary flows — elementary because they are the basic exchanges between the human world and the natural world. They are the only flows that score as environmental impact, because they are the only ones that actually reach the ecosphere.
Looking at those two emissions — Carbon dioxide and Methane — which one do you think causes more harm to the climate? Take a guess — there is no wrong answer here.
Student: carbon dioxide
AI: That is a very reasonable guess — carbon dioxide is the gas we hear about most often in climate discussions, so it feels like the obvious answer. And this study does emit more CO₂ by weight than methane: 2.5 kg of CO₂ compared to 0.4 kg of methane from the sheep farm.
But here is the surprising part: methane is actually the bigger climate problem in this study. Scientists have measured how powerfully each gas traps heat, and it turns out that one kilogram of methane traps about 28 times as much heat as one kilogram of CO₂. That methane comes from the sheep themselves — it is released during digestion, a process called enteric fermentation. The sheep burp and exhale it constantly, and every kilogram crosses the wall from the technosphere straight into the ecosphere.
So here is the what-if question: if the sheep farm stopped emitting methane entirely — same coal burned, same water used, same CO₂ released — but the methane crossing disappeared completely, how much of the total climate impact do you think would vanish? More than half, or less than half?
Student: more than half
AI: You are exactly right — and the actual number is striking. Once you apply that 28× multiplier to the methane, the maths looks like this:

Methane from the sheep farm: 0.44 kg × 28 = 12.3 kg CO₂ equivalent
Carbon dioxide from the farm: 0.55 kg CO₂ equivalent
Carbon dioxide from the mill: 2.0 kg CO₂ equivalent
Total: roughly 14.9 kg CO₂ equivalent per kilogram of wool yarn

The methane alone accounts for about 83% of the total climate impact — even though it looked like the smaller number on the page. Remove it, and nearly the entire footprint disappears. This is exactly why the ecosphere crossing matters more than the raw weight: a small amount of a potent gas crossing the wall can dwarf everything else in the study.
This has a direct lesson for anyone buying or sourcing wool. A supplier who focuses on reducing energy use at the mill — cutting the CO₂ from scouring and spinning — is tackling only 14% of the problem. The real hotspot is the sheep farm, and the real culprit is a gas that comes from the animals themselves. That is not easy to fix, but knowing where the crossing happens is the only way to know where to act.
The technosphere-ecosphere boundary is the reason LCA studies track elementary flows — that is the official name for the crossings we have been talking about. The next natural step is understanding how those flows get converted into impact scores — a process called characterisation, which is where that 28× multiplier actually comes from. Would you like to explore that, or is there anything about the two worlds you would like to look at more closely?

text:
lca_analysis.py builds a complete product system in openLCA from a recipe card, solves the technology matrix A, computes the scaling vector s = A⁻¹·f, and produces the LCI result B·s. It then does one of two things:

If the recipe card has an lcia: block with hand-typed characterization_factors, it multiplies B·s by those CFs in Python and reports impact scores.
If there is no lcia: block, it reports only raw CO₂.

Neither path uses openLCA’s own LCIA engine. No real LCIA method is attached to CalculationSetup. The database (paper_cup_lca) is empty — every flow, process, and unit is created from scratch on each run with fresh UUIDs.
This plan upgrades to a production-level system while keeping the matrix pedagogy fully intact.

text:
This document defines the format and content of the completed reference case studies used in this project. Each case study is a self-contained teaching package that provides enough information for an LLM-powered teaching skill to walk a student through any part of the LCA methodology using real numbers from that product.
The cases are designed for students at FIT (Fashion Institute of Technology) — business and retail management students with no programming background.




The reference teaching examples live in skills_references/ in the project root — separate from lca_analysis/, which holds examples tied to the openLCA server calculation workflow.

  cotton_fiber/

The teaching skills read from skills_references/<name>/ when given a case study argument. This keeps curated teaching material separate from ad-hoc analysis runs.

Folder: skills_references/wool_yarn/
Supply chain:
P1: Sheep farming  →  P2: Wool yarn production  [reference]
Depth: 1 layer. The sheep farm is one upstream node from the reference process. The scaling is straightforward: to produce 1 kg of yarn, you need 1.1 kg of raw fleece (10% waste in scouring and spinning), so the sheep farm runs at scale 1.1.

Folder: skills_references/cotton_fiber/
Supply chain:
P1: Fertilizer production  →  P2: Cotton farming  [reference]
Depth: 1 layer. Same structural depth as wool yarn — but this case introduces a second impact category, making the LCIA step the main teaching focus.
Emissions: - P1 (Fertilizer): CO2 (energy-intensive production of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer) - P2 (Cotton farming): CO2 (machinery, irrigation energy), N2O (from fertilised soil — microbial conversion of nitrogen), NH3 (volatilisation from soil)

title: Plan: Adding LCIA Methods and Database Support to the run-lca Skill
text:
The current run-lca skill and lca_analysis.py script build a complete product system in openLCA and run a calculation. However the calculation only returns raw inventory results — e.g. “0.1 kg CO₂ per cup”. It does not produce impact scores (GWP in kg CO₂-eq, DALYs, species-years, etc.) because no LCIA method is passed to the CalculationSetup.
In other words, the skill currently stops at Step 2 (Characterisation) of the LCIA chain. Steps 3 and 4 (damage modelling, endpoint scores) are not reached.






The recipe card format was designed from scratch to be readable for students. That was the right goal — but it was written without systematically checking every field against the olca-schema (the actual data format openLCA uses internally). Before extending the recipe card with new fields, we need to confirm that every existing field maps cleanly onto a real olca-schema concept, and identify any gaps or mismatches.
The olca-schema example files live at: https://github.com/GreenDelta/olca-schema/tree/master/examples



Every object in openLCA is a JSON file with a @type field, a UUID @id, and typed fields. Here are the key types relevant to the recipe card:
Process — one production step in the supply chain:
{
  "@type": "Process",
  "@id": "59963026-...",
  "name": "Steel production",
  "processType": "UNIT_PROCESS",
  "location": { "@type": "Location", "name": "Germany" },
  "exchanges": [ ... ]
}
Exchange — one input or output of a process:
{
  "@type": "Exchange",
  "internalId": 1,
  "amount": 1.0,
  "isInput": false,
  "isQuantitativeReference": true,
  "isAvoidedProduct": false,
  "flow": { "@type": "Flow", "name": "Steel" },
  "unit": { "@type": "Unit", "name": "kg" },
  "flowProperty": { "@type": "FlowProperty", "name": "Mass" }
}
Flow — a material, product, energy, or emission that moves between processes:
{
  "@type": "Flow",
  "name": "electricity, high voltage, at grid",
  "flowType": "PRODUCT_FLOW",
  "location": { "name": "Poland" },
  "flowProperties": [
    {
      "isRefFlowProperty": true,
      "flowProperty": { "name": "Energy" }
    }
  ]
}
Flow types are: PRODUCT_FLOW (technosphere), ELEMENTARY_FLOW (biosphere), or WASTE_FLOW.
UnitGroup — a family of related units with conversion factors:
{
  "@type": "UnitGroup",
  "name": "Units of energy",
  "units": [
    { "name": "MJ",  "isRefUnit": true,  "conversionFactor": 1.0 },
    { "name": "kWh", "isRefUnit": false, "conversionFactor": 3.6 }
  ]
}
ProductSystem — the full supply chain model:
{
  "@type": "ProductSystem",
  "name": "Ingot casting",
  "refProcess": { "name": "Ingot casting" },
  "refExchange": { "internalId": 1 },
  "targetAmount": 1.0,
  "targetUnit": { "name": "kg" },
  "processes": [ ... ],
  "processLinks": [ ... ]
}
ImpactCategory — one impact category with its characterisation factors:
{
  "@type": "ImpactCategory",
  "name": "Depletion of abiotic resources",
  "referenceUnitName": "kg antimony eq.",
  "impactFactors": [
    {
      "value": 1.09e-9,
      "flow": { "name": "Aluminium" },
      "unit": { "name": "kg" }
    }
  ]
}

Issue 1 — Unit groups are incorrectly structured
The recipe card has a flat units dict:
units:
  kWh: Energy
  kg:  Mass
  L:   Volume
The script currently creates one UnitGroup per symbol. But in the olca-schema, a UnitGroup is a family of interconvertible units — for example, {kg, g, t, lb} all belong to one “Units of mass” group with conversion factors. The current approach creates orphaned single-unit groups that don’t match any real database’s unit structure.
This matters because when linking foreground processes to background processes, unit names must match exactly. If the background database uses a “Units of mass” group containing kg with a standard UUID, and our script creates a separate “Mass units” group also containing kg, openLCA may treat them as different units.
Recommended fix: replace the flat units dict with a reference to standard unit groups. Either hard-code the standard openLCA unit group UUIDs in the script, or look them up from the database at runtime before creating any flows.
Issue 2 — No flowType distinction for resources vs emissions
Both resources and emissions are ELEMENTARY_FLOW in the schema. The difference is directionality: emissions are outputs from the technosphere to the biosphere (isInput: false), resources are inputs from the biosphere to the technosphere (isInput: true). The recipe card already captures this correctly via the emissions vs resources keys. No change needed — just confirming the mapping is right.
Issue 3 — No location field on flows or processes
Real background databases tag every process and product flow with a location (country or region). The recipe card has no location field. For toy models this does not matter. For real-world LCA it will matter because ecoinvent process names include the location (e.g. "market for electricity, low voltage | DE"). The source: background field (to be added) should handle this by using the full database process name, which includes the location.





Before adding any new features, fix the way the script creates unit groups so they match the standard openLCA structure. The script should:

Check whether the required unit groups already exist in the database (by looking up standard names like “Units of mass”, “Units of energy”, etc.).
If they exist (because a real database has been loaded), use them by reference — do not recreate them.
If they do not exist (fresh empty database, toy model), create them with the correct multi-unit structure including standard conversion factors.

lcia_method is functional — the script looks up this method by name and passes it to CalculationSetup.

Both fields are optional. If absent, the script runs inventory-only as today (backwards compatible).

        print(impact.impact_category.name,
              impact.amount,
              impact.impact_category.ref_unit)

Extend the recipe card to allow processes to be declared as coming from a loaded background database rather than defined locally:
processes:
  - name: P1 — Cut and sew shirt
    source: local                    # defined in this recipe card (default)
    reference_output: { flow: Shirt, amount: 1.0 }
    inputs:
      - { flow: Electricity, amount: 2.5 }

  - name: market for electricity, low voltage | DE
    source: background               # look up in the database by name
The script looks up background processes using:
provider = client.find(o.Process, "market for electricity, low voltage | DE")
and references them in the product system rather than creating them.
This requires a background process database to be loaded (US LCI, ELCD, etc.) — see Database Setup below.






The standard LCA teaching vocabulary (as used in the Constructing Inventories lecture slides) classifies every input and output of a unit process by a Type field:

Key insight: the unit process data tables shown in teaching slides (one table per process, with Name / Amount / Units / Type / Comments columns) are not the LCI result. They are the raw input data — equivalent to our recipe card. The LCI result is produced only after solving the technology matrix (A × s = f) and multiplying by the intervention matrix (g = B × s). The LCI result contains only elementary flows (Emissions + Resources); all Intermediate and Technosphere flows cancel out algebraically and disappear.

All existing recipe cards (coffee, cotton shirt, hand dryer, light bulb) explicitly model every upstream step — electricity generation is always its own process box. This means every entry in inputs has a matching reference_output somewhere in the same recipe card and therefore counts as Intermediate, not Technosphere. No inputs are silently dropped from the diagram.
This is a deliberate pedagogical choice: making every step visible helps students understand the full supply chain. It is also why the diagram always draws correctly — every arrow has both a source and a destination within the recipe card.
The Technosphere input distinction only becomes meaningful when background database support is added (see Step 3 below).







The olca-ipc Python client provides a method called create_product_system:
system_ref = client.create_product_system(
    process_ref,
    config=o.LinkingConfig(
        prefer_unit_processes=False,
        provider_linking=o.ProviderLinking.PREFER_DEFAULTS,
    )
)
This is openLCA’s auto-linking engine. When called, it:

Takes the reference (foreground) process as the starting point.
Scans every input of every foreground process for flows that have no supplier already defined within the foreground model.
Searches the entire database for any process whose reference output matches that flow (by flow name and unit).
If a match is found, links the background process into the product system.
Repeats recursively — the background process’s own inputs are also searched, pulling in further upstream processes until all inputs are satisfied or no more matches exist.

The result is a fully-linked ProductSystem object containing both the foreground processes (from the recipe card) and any background processes found in the database.



The technology matrix A and the subsequent scaling vector s cover every process in the product system — foreground and background alike. If ecoinvent has 20,000 processes and auto-linking pulls in 5,000 of them to satisfy the apple supply chain, then A is a 5,000×5,000 matrix and s has 5,000 entries. openLCA handles this internally; the student only sees the final aggregated LCI and LCIA results.



If create_product_system finds no supplier for a Technosphere input (because no background database is loaded), that input is left unlinked. The product system is incomplete. The calculation still runs but the results are partial — the upstream emissions from electricity, fertilizer, diesel etc. are missing. The script should warn the user in this case.



Before auto-linking, you can ask openLCA what is available:
# Find every process in the database that produces a given flow
flow_ref = o.Ref(name="Electricity, low voltage")
providers = client.get_providers(flow_ref)

text:
The recipe card format was designed from scratch to be readable for students. That was the right goal — but it was written without systematically checking every field against the olca-schema (the actual data format openLCA uses internally). Before extending the recipe card with new fields, we need to confirm that every existing field maps cleanly onto a real olca-schema concept, and identify any gaps or mismatches.
The olca-schema example files live at: https://github.com/GreenDelta/olca-schema/tree/master/examples



Every object in openLCA is a JSON file with a @type field, a UUID @id, and typed fields. Here are the key types relevant to the recipe card:
Process — one production step in the supply chain:
{
  "@type": "Process",
  "@id": "59963026-...",
  "name": "Steel production",
  "processType": "UNIT_PROCESS",
  "location": { "@type": "Location", "name": "Germany" },
  "exchanges": [ ... ]
}
Exchange — one input or output of a process:
{
  "@type": "Exchange",
  "internalId": 1,
  "amount": 1.0,
  "isInput": false,
  "isQuantitativeReference": true,
  "isAvoidedProduct": false,
  "flow": { "@type": "Flow", "name": "Steel" },
  "unit": { "@type": "Unit", "name": "kg" },
  "flowProperty": { "@type": "FlowProperty", "name": "Mass" }
}
Flow — a material, product, energy, or emission that moves between processes:
{
  "@type": "Flow",
  "name": "electricity, high voltage, at grid",
  "flowType": "PRODUCT_FLOW",
  "location": { "name": "Poland" },
  "flowProperties": [
    {
      "isRefFlowProperty": true,
      "flowProperty": { "name": "Energy" }
    }
  ]
}
Flow types are: PRODUCT_FLOW (technosphere), ELEMENTARY_FLOW (biosphere), or WASTE_FLOW.
UnitGroup — a family of related units with conversion factors:
{
  "@type": "UnitGroup",
  "name": "Units of energy",
  "units": [
    { "name": "MJ",  "isRefUnit": true,  "conversionFactor": 1.0 },
    { "name": "kWh", "isRefUnit": false, "conversionFactor": 3.6 }
  ]
}
ProductSystem — the full supply chain model:
{
  "@type": "ProductSystem",
  "name": "Ingot casting",
  "refProcess": { "name": "Ingot casting" },
  "refExchange": { "internalId": 1 },
  "targetAmount": 1.0,
  "targetUnit": { "name": "kg" },
  "processes": [ ... ],
  "processLinks": [ ... ]
}
ImpactCategory — one impact category with its characterisation factors:
{
  "@type": "ImpactCategory",
  "name": "Depletion of abiotic resources",
  "referenceUnitName": "kg antimony eq.",
  "impactFactors": [
    {
      "value": 1.09e-9,
      "flow": { "name": "Aluminium" },
      "unit": { "name": "kg" }
    }
  ]
}

Issue 1 — Unit groups are incorrectly structured
The recipe card has a flat units dict:
units:
  kWh: Energy
  kg:  Mass
  L:   Volume
The script currently creates one UnitGroup per symbol. But in the olca-schema, a UnitGroup is a family of interconvertible units — for example, {kg, g, t, lb} all belong to one “Units of mass” group with conversion factors. The current approach creates orphaned single-unit groups that don’t match any real database’s unit structure.
This matters because when linking foreground processes to background processes, unit names must match exactly. If the background database uses a “Units of mass” group containing kg with a standard UUID, and our script creates a separate “Mass units” group also containing kg, openLCA may treat them as different units.
Recommended fix: replace the flat units dict with a reference to standard unit groups. Either hard-code the standard openLCA unit group UUIDs in the script, or look them up from the database at runtime before creating any flows.
Issue 2 — No flowType distinction for resources vs emissions
Both resources and emissions are ELEMENTARY_FLOW in the schema. The difference is directionality: emissions are outputs from the technosphere to the biosphere (isInput: false), resources are inputs from the biosphere to the technosphere (isInput: true). The recipe card already captures this correctly via the emissions vs resources keys. No change needed — just confirming the mapping is right.
Issue 3 — No location field on flows or processes
Real background databases tag every process and product flow with a location (country or region). The recipe card has no location field. For toy models this does not matter. For real-world LCA it will matter because ecoinvent process names include the location (e.g. "market for electricity, low voltage | DE"). The source: background field (to be added) should handle this by using the full database process name, which includes the location.

They are the raw input data — equivalent to our recipe card. The LCI result is produced only after solving the technology matrix (A × s = f) and multiplying by the intervention matrix (g = B × s). text:
The olca-ipc Python client provides a method called create_product_system:
system_ref = client.create_product_system(
    process_ref,
    config=o.LinkingConfig(
        prefer_unit_processes=False,
        provider_linking=o.ProviderLinking.PREFER_DEFAULTS,
    )
)
This is openLCA’s auto-linking engine. When called, it:

Takes the reference (foreground) process as the starting point.
Scans every input of every foreground process for flows that have no supplier already defined within the foreground model.
Searches the entire database for any process whose reference output matches that flow (by flow name and unit).
If a match is found, links the background process into the product system.
Repeats recursively — the background process’s own inputs are also searched, pulling in further upstream processes until all inputs are satisfied or no more matches exist.

The result is a fully-linked ProductSystem object containing both the foreground processes (from the recipe card) and any background processes found in the database.



The technology matrix A and the subsequent scaling vector s cover every process in the product system — foreground and background alike. If ecoinvent has 20,000 processes and auto-linking pulls in 5,000 of them to satisfy the apple supply chain, then A is a 5,000×5,000 matrix and s has 5,000 entries. openLCA handles this internally; the student only sees the final aggregated LCI and LCIA results.



If create_product_system finds no supplier for a Technosphere input (because no background database is loaded), that input is left unlinked. The product system is incomplete. The calculation still runs but the results are partial — the upstream emissions from electricity, fertilizer, diesel etc. are missing. The script should warn the user in this case.



Before auto-linking, you can ask openLCA what is available:
# Find every process in the database that produces a given flow
flow_ref = o.Ref(name="Electricity, low voltage")
providers = client.get_providers(flow_ref)
for p in providers:
    print(p.process.name)
    # e.g. "market for electricity, low voltage | DE"
    #      "electricity production, wind, <1MW turbine, onshore | DE"
This is useful for verifying that a background database is loaded and for letting the student choose which provider to use when multiple options exist.
